articles.title: A strange twist in Alaska's Senate race has Trump's DOJ fighting to block results
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Justice Department's newly filed lawsuit to prevent Alaska state officials from certifying election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses in November. In an at-times contentious interview with CNN’s “State of the Union,” Blanche pointed out that according to the Constitution, Congress can create laws at any time to regulate elections. But when host Dana Bash asked what crime the administration was arguing was being committed, Blanche replied, “It depends.” “There could be a crime,” said Blanche. “But the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard. So an Alaskan intends to vote for one candidate, but is confused because of a second candidate with exactly the same name who has voted Democrat his entire life, who donated money to the other Democrat opponent, is running.” Bash pressed Blanche on how it is illegal for two candidates with the same name to be on a ballot at the same time. "It is an obligation of the states to avoid confusion, among other things, confusion in the minds of voters in the election process,” Blanche replied. “So the question is whether Alaska, by allowing this to happen, is violating the law and the federal law and the constitution by allowing confusion in the ballot." The Alaskan Supreme Court in June ruled that both Sullivans may remain on the ballot as the incumbent faces off in a tight reelection battle with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The four-person Senate ranked-choice ballot for the general election specifies that Dan S. Sullivan is a "Registered Republican" and the "incumbent" — no information is listed after Dan J. Sullivan Jr's name. Regardless, in the suit filed Thursday , DOJ argued that Dan J. Sullivan Jr.’s name on the ballot constitutes a purposeful effort to mislead voters. In an interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) argued the administration has no standing to bring the lawsuit, and he lambasted Blanche for leading a “disgraceful campaign.” “This suit has no chance of succeeding,” said Schiff. “But the fact that Todd Blanche and the Justice Department are willing to go along with it, they're willing to put their name on it, is an indication of how far they will go after this election is over to try to challenge the results.” Still, it’s unclear how much the court can do about the Justice Department’s lawsuit. With ballots secret, it is virtually impossible for the Justice Department to identify specific voters and clarify which Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for. Blanche, though, seemed unconcerned about that hurdle. “There are a number of scenarios where it could be obvious that a voter was confused by the way they wrote down candidates,” said Blanche. Republican groups have worked to differentiate between the two Sullivans . President Donald Trump on Friday said the legal challenge was his idea, though Blanche on Sunday declined to state whether the president had directed him to file the suit. "I will never talk about any communications I have with the president of the United States,” he said. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who is not up for reelection this year, said Friday that the lawsuit is unnecessary. “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” Murkowski said in a post on X . “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.” Her comments drew the ire of Trump, who on Saturday called Murkowski “Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far,” in a post to Truth Social . Trump said that Alaska’s ranked choice voting system is “a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.” “He is only there because the Democrats want to steal the Election, and Murkowski probably wants that to happen, which is why she is against the DOJ filing a Lawsuit in order to stop this impending crime and tragedy,” Trump added. “I have delivered for Alaska at Historic Levels, nobody has ever seen anything like it, and all I’m asking for is a FAIR AND HONEST SENATORIAL ELECTION! Lisa Murkowski is a DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country. You just don’t get any worse!" Democratic leaders have also widely condemned the lawsuit, arguing the president is attempting to lay the foundation to overturn the midterm election results if their candidates win critical elections — something Bash asked Blanche about on Sunday. “One of the big questions is whether or not the president is laying the groundwork for a scenario where, whether it's Alaska or somewhere else, there is, in your words a couple of days ago, a 'doomsday scenario' and we could be in a situation where President Trump tries to overturn the election and the result of that could be, god forbid, what we saw after January 6th,” Bash said. Blanche quickly fired back: “Oh stop it. You gotta stop it with that. You're not being a real person. You set me up. You're saying, “'Mr. Attorney General, because the president of the United States wants to stop fraud and confusion in Alaska, is he going to do something crazy?' That is not a real question.” Bash replied that she did not think it was an unfair question, but Blanche argued that the premise of the question was untrue. “Instead of focusing on how we can address that and how we can remedy that, you're talking about January 6th,” he said. “That's so embarrassing to this network that that's what you're talking about.” “Oh, come on,” Bash said. "Don't “oh, come on” me,” replied Blanche. “There's literally confusion." Blanche denied any political motivations were behind the Justice Department’s lawsuit. “It's important the American people understand that we are not — President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape or form,” he said. “What we're trying to do is make it clear that if it is obvious after the election, that confusion led to an improper and illegal result that the Alaskan system should be able to address that.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/25/blanche-alaska-lawsuit-could-be-crime-01134861

articles.title: Trump announces $4 billion Audi factory in Georgia ahead of midterms
articles.summary: By Bo Erickson, David Shepardson and Rachel More PERRY, Georgia/BERLIN, Oct 25 (Reuters) - The head of German automaker Audi defended on Sunday the company's planned $4 billion investment in a new US plant, announced by President Donald Trump as he campaigns for the November midterm ‌elections. Audi Chief Executive Gernot Doellner stood alongside Trump at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia on Saturday, as the ‌US president said Audi, part of the Volkswagen Group, planned to build an assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually. "This decision was preceded by many months of careful ​planning and intense negotiations," Doellner told reporters on Sunday. "If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands." A final decision on the investment will have to be taken by Volkswagen's supervisory board for it to go ahead. Georgia has competitive election races for the US Senate and its governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy ‌and boosting US manufacture. In Germany, the tariffs have added ⁠to the pressures on European industry and tension between Volkswagen management and workers, who face job cuts and possible plant closures. Trump's tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and parts cost Audi around €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) last year as it imports all ⁠its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico, Audi has said. Critics of the tariffs say they have also been damaging in the US where they have increased vehicle prices and delayed some automaker investments. A spokesperson for Germany's IG Metall union said the decision by Doellner to extend a hand to Trump during the election ​was "hard ​to understand". "Trump has never failed to make it clear what he is after: he wants ​to weaken our domestic economy, particularly the automotive sector," the ‌spokesperson said. Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair, said it was "right and necessary" to improve the company's position on the US market with a new plant. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out," she said. Doellner declined to give full details on the investment deal with the US, including whether it involves tariff relief for the company. AN OPPORTUNITY IF GERMAN WORKERS BENEFIT Olaf Lies, state premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an ‌opportunity provided German workers also benefit. "Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here ​and must not displace them," he said. Audi said the investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. ​Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in ​the early 2030s, Audi said. The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official ‌told Reuters. Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year ​in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. ​Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a $2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said. "We regard the region as ​a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver ‌Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this." A gold Audi with manufacturer licence plates was parked ​outside Trump's rally on Saturday. (Reporting by Bo Erickson in Perry and David Shepardson in Washington; Additional reporting by Christoph Steitz and ​Rachel More; Editing by Nia Williams, Rod Nickel, David Goodman and Barbara Lewis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/trump-set-announce-plan-audi-213133434.html

articles.title: She blocked his bid to become a federal judge. Now he's running for her Senate seat.
articles.summary: Why are major Democrats and Republicans flocking to Mississippi in recent weeks? In a climate where polls show President Donald Trump's approval ratings cratering, Democrats are unusually optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping the Senate seat held by incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith -- even in deep-red Mississippi. "We got to have a senator that looks out for Mississippi, that puts Mississippi farmers first, Mississippi small businesses first, represent our values by not allowing corruption to ruin our country and actually delivers on the commitments to put America first," Colom told ABC News in an interview earlier this week. Sarah Warnock/AP Photo - PHOTO: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks during a voting rights town hall at the historic Farish Street Baptist Church in Jackson, Miss., Aug. 1, 2026. The incumbent's campaign dismisses the Democratic push as the last-ditch effort of a campaign that will fall short. Gov. Wes Moore says key races in South 'in play,' Democrats 'made mistakes' not investing earlier Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. Democrats have argued that Colom's prominent credentials, as well as voter pushback against Republican incumbents and motivation among Democratic-leaning Black voters, could help boost him. Mississippi's population is around 36% Black, according to U.S. Census data . Colom faces an uphill battle, as Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 and voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by around 20 points. ABC News rates the race solid Republican. But he has gotten the attention of national Democrats; major party figures such as former former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock have campaigned with him. Former President Barack Obama also recorded an ad for him released earlier this month. Harris, during a rally with Colom on Thursday, told attendees, "I've been in those rooms where there's no cameras, it's senators talking to each other... When you have a voice like his in that room, just think about the impact that's going to have on the decisions coming out of that room. Think about that. This is no ordinary time, and this is no ordinary man." AP Photo - PHOTO: Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigns for candidate Scott Colom in Mississippi, Oct. 22, 2026. Colom also went viral online last week after a social video he posted showed Hyde-Smith, during a local news interview from February, saying "You have so many proteins to choose from" while discussing how to deal with higher prices on meat and other goods. In the interview, Hyde-Smith also spoke about working on regulations that would help energy production, and tax incentives to help development. But it was the proteins part that Colom's campaign seized on, with a punchy video that featured voters mocking the senator's words, with one saying, "Pick another protein ... I'd rather pick another Senator instead." (The campaign has confirmed to ABC News that the video has been turned into a campaign ad.) Sarah Warnock/AP Photo - PHOTO: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom listens during a maternal health roundtable at the Capital Club in Jackson, Miss., Aug. 1, 2026. One concrete sign of confidence among Democrats over Colom's chances came on Tuesday, when the Senate Majority PAC, an outside group aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on an ad campaign across broadcast TV and digital for ads for Colom. Asked what signs the group sees in Mississippi that makes it worth investing in, spokesperson Lauren French wrote, "Cindy Hyde-Smith has spent a decade in Washington without passing a single piece of legislation, and Mississippians have noticed." Hyde-Smith has cosponsored legislation that has passed into law but legislation she initially sponsored or reintroduced has not become law, according to congressional records . Asked to respond to Senate Majority PAC, Hyde-Smith's campaign pointed to how bills from lawmakers "are often passed as part of larger legislative packages," and that has been true for some of Hyde-Smith's bills, including the first one she introduced. The campaign also pointed out that she is running for only her second full term. French said Colom is running a "disciplined campaign" with messages resonating with voters. Colom and Hyde-Smith have some history, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023. She cited his support for transgender rights and having previously been boosted by a George Soros-linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press . He insists his bid for Senate is not motivated by a desire to get back at her. "It has nothing to do with the run for me ... as a Christian, I forgive her. It's about the people in Mississippi," Colom told ABC News. Hyde-Smith dismissed Colom's chances. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images - PHOTO: Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith arrives in the U.S. Capitol for the first vote of the week, September 22, 2026. "We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith back to the U.S. Senate on November 3rd. This is simply Washington insiders making a last ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign," campaign manager Jake Monssen told ABC News in a statement. Hyde-Smith's supporters may be more motivated after a boost from President Donald Trump, who's set to hold a rally in Mississippi on Monday as part of a swing of campaign rallies mostly in red states. The Republican National Committee announced the rally around a week after Colom's social video went viral, although Trump and the group have not indicated why they are doing the rally there and Trump has expressed confidence in Hyde-Smith. "Cindy Hyde-Smith's very popular ... So if I need to get her over the top, I would go there [to Mississippi]. She's great. Cindy Hyde-Smith is great," Trump told reporters when asked Thursday about the Senate election. Hyde-Smith will be attending the rally, according to her campaign. articles.title: These Trump voters have soured on his presidency — and could be key to the midterms
articles.summary: The midterm campaign is being fought in areas President Donald Trump carried in the last election, and largely among voters who have supported him in the past but have soured on his presidency. Rick Sebring, a resident of rural Black Creek, Georgia, is one of them. He was among the Americans drawn to Trump when he emerged as a political outsider running for president in 2015, and supported him in each election since. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Now, he says, he jokes with his son and daughter, 25 and 18, that he needs a hat that reads: "I fell for it three times." Trump is "not the same guy he was before," said Sebring, 66, who explained that he no longer believes the president is acting with ordinary Americans' best interests at heart. "It's kind of like if your wife is screwing the guy next door," Sebring said. "You know, you're kind of butt hurt about it." He is furious about the war against Iran that Trump started after pledging to avoid new wars in the Middle East. Trump should tell Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom the president endorsed for reelection last week, to "go to hell," Sebring said, and "cut off all aid" to Israel and Ukraine. He is bothered that Trump tried to stop the release of the Epstein files. He is disappointed that the government-slashing DOGE program, which Trump appointed Elon Musk to run, was ultimately brought to a halt. Sebring, who responded to the most recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll and agreed to a follow-up interview, is part of a small but potentially crucial slice of this year's electorate. About 1 in 5 registered voters who cast ballots for Trump in 2024, 22 percent, now disapprove of the job he's doing. They make up about 8 percent of the electorate. They're not natural Democratic voters - the vast majority identify as Republicans or independents - but this year, many of them, like Sebring, say they will cast a vote for the opposing party. Republicans have hoped to woo some of them back. If that fails, however, the election could become a Democratic rout, both partisan and nonpartisan analysts say. The voters who have turned against Trump are a mix of longtime, once-loyal supporters and those who joined his coalition for the first time in 2024. They're more divided than those who cast ballots for Kamala Harris about who should control the next Congress, according to the poll. Nearly all of the people who voted for Harris in 2024, 99 percent, say they would like to see the next Congress controlled by Democrats "to act as a check on Trump," the poll found. Among voters who sided with Trump in 2024, a large majority do say they would prefer a Republican Congress "to support Trump's agenda," but about 1 in 7 say they favor Democratic control. To date, Sebring has voted for one Democrat in his life - former Alabama governor Don Siegelman, who ran in 1998 on bringing the lottery to the state - but said "that is going to change in November," when he plans to vote for Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Georgia). Others say they'll split their ticket or stay home. Carrie Bacon, a 73-year-old retired nurse in Belfast, Maine, voted for Trump in the past because she didn't want to see his Democratic challengers win the presidency. Now, she refers to him as "the bozo that's currently in the White House," saying he's "after his own aggrandizement and making as much money on the side as he can." Bacon, who responded to a Washington Post-Schar School poll of her state, said she will vote for Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) because the longtime incumbent has shown she can act independently of her party. But she will not support the Republican running in her congressional district, former Maine governor Paul LePage. Russell Clements, a 61-year-old retiree and three-time Trump voter from Gloucester, Virginia, who responded to a Post-Schar School poll in his state, said he soured on the president after watching how he handled the Iran war. Even so, Clements said that if he could go back to 2024, he would still not vote for the Democrat. He isn't sure that he'll vote in this year's midterm elections, and he suspects that if Democrats take back Congress, they'll prioritize impeaching Trump over legislating. "I don't see where that serves any purpose," Clements said. "He's going to be gone in two years anyway." Jill Vandermolen, a 56-year-old teacher in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin, who responded to the Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, said she voted for Trump three times as the lesser of two evils and because she had family members who were excited about his reputation as a businessman. She, too, says she may not vote this year. "Everything costs more money," she said. As for Trump, she said that she does "not have faith in him at all." The poll found that 76 percent of Trump voters nationwide who still approve of the president's performance either were certain to vote or have already done so. By contrast, among Trump voters who now disapprove of him, just 53 percent said they are either certain to vote or already have. Historically, one of the strongest predictors of how a person will vote in midterm elections is their approval or disapproval of the president's job performance. That's because midterm elections typically act as a referendum on the party in the White House. The challenge for Republicans is that Trump's approval, which was already low earlier this year, has continued to drop as the midterm elections approach. His approval was 39 percent among registered voters in the Post poll in February, 37 percent in July and 33 percent in the current survey. That decline, which has been seen in many other surveys as well, has largely come among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents. Nearly all Democrats already disapproved of him. Trump's approval rating is significantly lower than it was during the midterm election of his first term, in 2018, when Democrats made sizable gains. His standing rivals the lows set by Presidents Harry S. Truman in 1946 and George W. Bush in 2006, whose parties suffered major defeats. Not all Trump voters who have soured on him are going to punish Republicans in the midterms, however, seeing the Democrats as a worse option. Efforts to motivate those voters by highlighting issues on which they dislike Democrats have been at the core of Trump's campaign rallies all month. Amy Reese, 42, of Victoria, Virginia, said she has "never seen the economy this bad, ever, and it's scary." She has supported Trump in each election - and would again - but more recently has been horrified when she sees him on TV, "and he's like, 'Oh, the economy is so good.'" Last month, her family's electric bill was almost $700. The cost she's paying each month for insulin as a Type 1 diabetic has more then doubled. Her husband drives for a living selling wholesale to convenience stores, and if Trump doesn't do something quickly about gas prices, "he is going to put a lot of small-business owners out of business, my husband one of them," she said. Trump's promised $5,000 checks if Republicans win the elections "aren't enough" to make up for the hardship people have faced this year, and besides, Reese said, those checks would never get approved by Congress. But Reese will vote Republican in the midterms, she says, explaining that she "will never vote for a Democrat," primarily because she opposes abortion. Dana Bessen, 76, of Highland, Michigan, also voted for Trump three times, despite not having a high opinion of him. The retired engineering technician disapproves of most everything the president has done during his second term, particularly his trade policy. Bessen said, however, that he'll still vote for Republicans in the midterms. "They're not Trump," he said. Post Polling Director Scott Clement contributed to this report. articles.title: Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
articles.summary: So far in President Trump's second term, prices in the US have risen only about half as quickly compared to his predecessor's four years in office. Yet Trump has a 72% disapproval rating on the issue and risks paying a steep political price — just as former President Joe Biden did — with voters drawing a direct connection between rising prices and the president's policies. In the last election cycle, prices of all items rose more than 20% during Biden's term , sparking widespread voter angst. This time around, price growth is notably slower, rising 5.4% in a little less than two years since Inauguration Day. But a Yahoo Finance analysis of price data shows that a few major outliers have hit Americans' wallets in an outsized way, largely due to increases in goods affected by the war in Iran and tariffs. Fuel oil and gasoline are perhaps the most dramatic examples, spiking over 30% beginning in March in response to the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz. And voters have noticed, as evidenced in poll after poll. A New York Times/Siena poll released this week found 73% of likely voters disapprove of the president's handling of gas prices. Trump underscored the salience of energy prices when he posted a charge this week that "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election." Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the Iran war ends. Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries Link between price spikes and Trump policies The connection between price increases and Trump's tariff policy has also been in evidence. Coffee prices have risen nearly 23% during Trump's second term (more than double the rate under Biden) as tariffs raised prices before Trump scrapped many of the coffee duties late last year in response to coffee drinkers' unhappiness. Goods like toys and footwear have likewise risen rapidly as importers from China and elsewhere in Asia faced new tariffs. Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term. "Maybe the children will have two dolls instead of 30 dolls, and maybe the two dolls will cost a couple of bucks more than they would normally," Trump said in a rare acknowledgment of tariff-fueled price increases when he was pressed on the issue in April. Other goods have moved in the opposite direction. Eggs jumped by an average of 2.57% each month when Biden was in the White House, but have dropped 3.82% each month of Trump's term so far, the analysis shows. But tariffs remain in focus and unpopular, with an average of polls from the Silver Bulletin finding that 62.7% of Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled trade and tariffs versus 32.8% who approve. President Donald Trump is seen after a rally on October 22 in Sioux City, Iowa.. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images Gas in focus in the final weeks of the campaign Despite the different roots, inflation has emerged as the central political problem for Trump and his party — as it was for Biden and Democrats — and comes as early voting is already underway for the Nov. 3 midterms. And perhaps no individual price tag is more politically charged, for any president, than the cost of a gallon of gas. Trump is trying to make his case as gas prices are averaging about $4.30 per gallon and diesel is elevated after setting an all-time price record last month, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Trump has taken multiple actions just this week to try to rein in prices, including $8 billion in support for farmers and invoking the Defense Production Act on Thursday to direct new funds to increase refining capacity. Yahoo Finance Trump touted the moves before voters in Iowa on Thursday , saying the release of $150 million would lead to more production of diesel and gasoline. Yet he faces the inconvenient fact that his record on gas prices is now all but indistinguishable from Biden's. Since Jan. 20, 2025, prices have averaged $3.449 per gallon according to data from the Energy Information Administration . Under Biden, the average price was $3.455 per gallon over his four years. Trump spent much of the last campaign promising the opposite, pledging $ 2 per gallon gasoline and vanishing inflation in nearly every 2024 campaign speech. That is leading voters to blame the president for the state of affairs. This week's national poll from the New York Times and Siena University found that 75% of voters view economic conditions as only fair or poor, and a solid majority put the blame on Trump. As Ipsos also put it this week in a summary of recent findings :  "Americans' confidence in the economy has been bad since the Iran war began [and] now the bottom has dropped out." articles.title: U.S. Marine indicted on robbery and murder charges in Japanese woman's death in Okinawa
articles.summary: A US marine has been indicted in Okinawa prefecture in Japan on charges of robbing and murdering a Japanese woman. Lance corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was accused of killing Anna Yagi, 39 , in a hotel in the prefecture ’s capital Naha and taking her wallet and backpack earlier this month. Ballard denied the allegations. Ballard, who was stationed at Futenma Air Base, was found walking alone in Okinawa city later that day and was arrested the following day on suspicion of robbery and murder. He was indicted on Sunday amid growing anger among Okinawa residents over the incident and the presence of US military installations. He allegedly strangled the woman with the cord of a telephone in a hotel room between 2.10 and 4.15am on 3 October and stole her backpack that contained her wallet and other belongings, according to the indictment. The woman had checked into the hotel with a man around 2.10am that day. Hotel employees entered the room at 4.15am after she did not check out on time. The staff found her body and alerted the police, investigative sources told the Japan Times . Ballard, pictured leaving a police station, denies the allegations (Reuters) Investigators later checked the security footage that showed a man with tattoos on both arms and a backpack leading the hotel, the report said. The backpack was found near the hotel. Under Japanese law, conviction can carry the death penalty or life imprisonment. The incident involving a foreign national prompted Okinawa governor Genta Koja to step up calls for the central government to take preventive measures. Local residents have long voiced anger over crimes committed by US military personnel, including offences against women and girls, as well as noise and pollution associated with American military installations. Following his arrest, the US military in Okinawa imposed a 30-day curfew on 9 October, restricting personnel from leaving their bases between midnight and 5 am. It was after the Japanese government lodged a strong protest with the US government over the incident. Prime minister Sanae Takaichi condemned the incident as a “brutal and heinous” crime and called for stricter discipline of American personnel. People watch the flight line near a poster showing the different kinds of aircraft next to Kadena Air Base in Kadena, Okinawa prefecture (AFP/Getty) The incident renewed long-standing local tensions over the heavy US military presence on Okinawa, which hosts a large share of US bases in Japan. Crimes involving US military personnel stationed in Japan, including murder, rape, and robbery, have long been a source of public concern. In Okinawa, local police handled over 100 criminal cases involving US personnel in 2025 alone, according to an official from the prefecture. In 2016, a former Marine and Kadena base civilian worker Kenneth Gadson was sentenced to life in prison for raping and murdering a 20-year-old woman. The rape of a ​12-year-old Okinawan ⁠girl by three US servicemen in 1995 sparked widespread protests. articles.title: Ukraine is using drones like Wi-Fi extenders to help its attack drones fly farther
articles.summary: Twist Robotics' drones can be used as signal repeaters to help the connection between a drone operator and their mission drone. Twist Robotics Drones in Ukraine act as flying communications bridges between operators and mission drones. They repeat the operators' signal to allow drones to fly farther while staying connected. The signal-repeating drones make other drones more resistant to Russia's electronic warfare. Ukraine has created drones that act as flying relay towers, allowing its drones conducting missions to fly farther while making them harder for Russia to jam. In a war where drones gather intel and account for more than 95% of Russia's front-line losses , Ukraine wants its operators to keep control of their drones over longer distances with stronger signals that are harder for Russia to break. One solution is the signal repeater drone, a flying signal booster that operates between a pilot and a mission drone, relaying commands to the aircraft and sending back video and intelligence to the operator. Able to fly much higher than a ground antenna, airborne repeaters can extend a drone's range and help preserve the connection under pressure. It increases the mission drone's operational range by extending how far it can fly while staying connected to its pilot. It's a similar principle to how wifi repeaters work. Ukrainian arms maker Twist Robotics makes a signal-repeating drone, born from its Saker Scout drone. Rostyslav Olenchyn, the company's co-founder and chief information officer, told Business Insider that the drone was widely used for reconnaissance and strike operations, but this war changes rapidly , with arms and warfighting technology quickly becoming obsolete. And without updates, this drone was at risk of falling victim to that pattern in the cat-and-mouse technology race. Drones needed to be effective at longer ranges, and the Saker Scout's range was "not enough" for many missions. So, the drone was redesigned "for another objective. It became the signal relay station," Olenchyn said. Ukraine's drone operators want to be able to fly their drones as far and with as strong a connection as possible. Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images The Saker Scout, able to also be used in other combat roles, can extend the operational range of drones by more than 50 kilometers, according to the company. The concept of using aircraft as signal middlemen isn't new. Militaries have used helicopters and planes to relay communications between assets and forces disconnected by the terrain, though usually troops rather than drones. These crewed aircraft, however, struggle to operate over Ukraine , but while such air assets are few and far between, drones are prolific. Large crewed aircraft cannot "necessarily survive in the heavy saturated air of the battlefield," where drones and air defenses are a threatening presence, Olenchyn said. "So the small, versatile platform was a solution." He said that serial production of the Saker Scout with this function started in 2023. The company's strike drone, the Signal Hunter, can also be used as a relay. Other Ukrainian companies are also working in the space, with some updating existing drone types and some designing new ones. Roboneers, for example, developed a version of its Wardog drone that can carry relay equipment weighing up to three kilograms, and Skyriper makes the Skyriper-R Airborne Repeater, a dedicated drone with the single function of acting as an airborne repeater. Volodymyr Zinovskyi, the CEO of the Ukrainian defense firm TAF Industries, told Business Insider that his company started making relay drones last year at the request of units, describing the technology as going from optional to essential. Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, wrote last year that "the use of UAVs over long distances or in difficult terrain requires the use of repeaters - special devices that help increase the range of a stable signal several times." Some Ukrainian drones are built for this relay mission, while others can be fitted with add-on repeater equipment. Twist Robotics' Saker Scout repeats the signal from a drone operator to their mission drone, and the reverse. Twist Robotics Beyond overcoming geographical challenges, airborne repeaters also help counter Russian electronic warfare by strengthening the communications link between operators and mission drones, making it harder to disrupt, though Russia can still target the relay itself. An analysis published by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank, last year described the creation of relay systems as a response to growing electronic warfare tactics, including the ability that both sides have to trace drone control signals back to their source for strikes on operators, priority targets in this war. Dmytro "Liber" Zhluktenko, a former drone operator who now serves as a lessons-learned analyst with Ukraine's 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment "RAID," told Business Insider that Ukrainian forces are "keeping somewhat a stable radio link by mass utilizing signal repeaters." He said that some uncrewed repeater aircraft are fixed-wing drones, while some are repurposed bomber-type drones. Instead of bombs, it just carries the signal repeater," he said. "We optimize those signal repeater carriers to just stay in the air for an extremely long time, like one hour plus," he said. "That's their only job: to be in the air." Working with strike drones, they give operators a "great radio link over the target." Oleksiy, the commander of the 2nd UAV engineer platoon of the International Defense Legion of Ukraine, told ArmyInform, the official information agency of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, last year that his unit uses repeaters on drones to expand the radio horizon of the drones they want to use and fly further to target Russia. Russia is using the technology too, including to help attack drones fly deeper into Ukrainian territory. And these lessons aren't limited to the Ukraine war. The US military is also experimenting with ways to extend drone operations and keep operators connected from farther away. The Marine Corps, for instance, has experimented with using helicopters as FPV motherships, as well as handing off control after launch . Though different from Ukraine's airborne repeater work, both address a similar battlefield problem, which is that drones are only useful if operators can launch them, control them, and keep receiving information at tactically relevant distances. Olenchyn said that updates, like the signal repeating ability, are critical in combat. He said that every two weeks, the company has "a new update, new kinds of techniques, new kinds of drones or functionality which are released." If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo. articles.title: Amy Acton urges Trump and Vance to 'look at the facts' after Ramaswamy attack ad
articles.summary: Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton told ABC News in an interview Saturday that she hopes President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance will "look at the facts" of the abuse she says she endured as a child after they defended an attack ad made by GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign. Bipartisan backlash has hit Ramaswamy's campaign, after the release of the ad featuring Acton's estranged mother who Acton says stood by the man who was criminally charged with sexually abusing her as a child. Acton said she hasn't seen her mother since she was 12 years old. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, said Acton has lied about her past, though it doesn't mention the allegations of sexual abuse. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Amy Acton In response to Trump and Vance who have doubled down on and defended the ad, Acton told ABC News, "My job is to work with anyone on any side of the aisle to solve problems instead of making them, and I would say I do hope they would look at the facts." Acton spoke to ABC News after a rally in Cleveland with former President Barack Obama. Trump doubles down on Amy Acton criticism as Ramaswamy ad controversy swirls Acton has alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him. He pleaded not guilty, but fled the state before trial and never appeared before a judge. He died in 2004. Shannon Stapleton/Reuters - PHOTO: Ohio Midterm Elections Acton said she and her brother endured "extreme child abuse and neglect" in their childhood. "We were frequent flyers in children's services ... There are facts in this case: a grand jury indictment, fugitive out against bail, and that behavior went on and on," Acton said. Speaking to reporters this week about the ad, Trump dismissed questions about the allegations of Acton's sexual abuse, asserting at multiple points that the ad has "nothing to do" with Acton's stepfather. Spencer Platt/Getty Images - PHOTO: Ohio Republican Candidates Campaign At The Circleville Pumpkin Show Rally Similarly, Vance told rally attendees in Ohio earlier this week that he is "a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America." GOP Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who on Thursday told reporters in Columbus, Ohio, that the ad is "deeply, deeply troubling" and that the Ramaswamy campaign "needs to take it down," but he did not withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy. Asked whether she was disappointed that DeWine didn't withdraw his endorsement, Acton said it was "an honor and a privilege" to work with him during COVID-19 pandemic as the director of the Ohio Department of Health. Vance praises Ramaswamy for having 'audacity' to run controversial Amy Acton ad "I really do appreciate him calling out the facts of the case," Acton said. "That this was an indictment he knows better than others. He's a prosecutor. He started his career prosecuting cases like this, and he knew more than anyone. He knows who I am and knows my story." Speaking to reporters on Friday, Ramaswamy said the ad had nothing to do with childhood abuse. "We ran an ad about lying," he said. "Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me, about her record, about her history in this state." In a statement to ABC News, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy said: "Ohioans can't afford a liberal governor who shows up for Obama but never shows up for them." Ramaswamy and Acton have never met in person. Asked what she would say to him, Acton said: "I really have no words for Mr. Ramaswamy. I think there is no low that he wouldn't sink to." Speaking to survivors of abuse, Acton said: "For those out there going through it now, hold on, please. If there's someone you feel safe with, say something about it." Obama blasts Trump, says Ramaswamy 'thirsty' for attention Acton campaigned Saturday alongside former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who's running to win back his seat, and Obama, who was the last Democratic presidential candidate to win the state of Ohio in a presidential election in 2012. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Amy Acton,Barack Obama,Sherrod Brown Democrats are eyeing the Senate and gubernatorial races as key pickup opportunities given the headwinds facing Republicans. Amy Acton campaign slams Ramaswamy over controversial ad featuring estranged mother In his remarks, Obama delivered a scathing rebuke of the Trump administration on a variety of issues — from the economy to immigration to the war in Iran. Regarding the GOP candidate for governor, Obama called Ramaswamy "thirsty" for attention. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Election 2026 Ohio Senate "Vivek's own supporters know it's all about what's in it for him," Obama said. "We all know that guy, you know, who ... just wants to get attention no matter what, willing to do anything. And in recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to." Obama emphasized what he called a "moral component" to this election and said that "basic decency" is missing from the current public discourse. ABC News' Diana Paulsen contributed to this report. articles.title: 12 people shot, including children, after Florida A&M homecoming game
articles.summary: At least 12 people, half of them juveniles and the youngest just 11 years old, were injured in a mass shooting near FAMU’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night amid homecoming weekend. Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said 11 people suffered gunshot wounds. Three victims were seriously injured, including one in critical condition, while eight were stable. A FAMU student was among the injured. Police said preliminary information indicates an altercation occurred between individuals before the shooting, which Revell called an "isolated incident." The latest: FAMU homecoming ends with one of city's worst mass shootings; six victims still hospitalized Midnight update: At least 12 injured in Perry Street shooting; youngest victim is 11 At least 12 people were injured, including six juveniles, in the shooting near FAMU’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night, Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said at a late-night press conference. “I stand before you tonight devastated,” Revell said. Eleven of the victims suffered gunshot wounds. Six victims are adults and six are juveniles, with the youngest just 11 years old, Revell said. A twelfth victim is the grandmother of one of the victims who was injured fleeing from the scene. He said one of the victims is a FAMU student. Three victims suffered serious injuries and one was in critical condition. Eight were in stable condition. He spoke directly to the victims and their families: "We hurt with you, and we will continue to get you the answers you so desperately want." The shooting occurred just before 8 p.m. near Perry and Manatee streets. Preliminary information indicates an altercation occurred between individuals before the shooting, Revell said. No one has been arrested at this time. Revell said investigators believe this was an "isolated incident between two or three individuals and nothing more than that." He asked anyone who saw anything or knows anything to come forward with information. Anyone with information is asked to call TPD at 850-891-4200 or Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS. More information will be released as it becomes available. "My message to the community is this... No family should have to experience this kind of violence, this kind of fear, this kind of heartbreak," he said. Revell took a moment to recognize "some of the heroic efforts" of first responders. "We had officers who were picking up victims and carrying them in their arms to transport because they couldn't get through the mass of people," he said. While choking up, he said it's critical for crowds to disperse so officers can get to victims. "Without hesitation they ran into the middle of this, still not knowing where the shooters were, still not knowing how many victims they had. They ran into the middle of this and put themselves in harms way." After midnight, Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey posted on x that “this is a truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy.” “Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone,” he wrote. “Our entire community stands with you.” 11:22 p.m. TPD and FAMU to hold press conference The Tallahassee Police Department and Florida A&M University Police Department will hold a press conference at 11:30 p.m. Saturday to provide updates on the Perry Street incident. The briefing will be held on FAMU’s campus at 1845 Althea Gibson Way. The announcement comes as authorities continue investigating the shooting near Bragg Memorial Stadium. Police previously said there were victims, but the number of people injured and the extent of their injuries remained unknown. The Tallahassee Democrat livestreamed it here. 11:10 p.m. FAMU issues statement: 'Our hearts go out to the victims and all those affected' At about 11 p.m., Florida A&M University issued a statement on the shooting through a Sachs Media representative sharing its condolences and saying the "campus remains safe." “The University is aware of an incident that occurred near campus on Perry Street on the evening of October 24. The Tallahassee Police Department is on the scene and actively investigating the situation." “Our hearts go out to the victims and all those affected by this tragic incident. While the campus remains safe, individuals are encouraged to avoid the area to allow law enforcement to conduct its investigation." “The safety and security of our students, faculty, and staff remain our highest priority. We are closely monitoring the situation and will share additional updates as more information becomes available. Anyone who has information about the situation is encouraged to contact the Tallahassee Police Department.” Anyone with information is asked to call TPD at 850-891-4200 or Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS. More information will be released as it becomes available. 10:30 p.m.: Social media videos show scenes of chaos Video of the shooting and its aftermath are circulating on social media. One video viewed by tens of thousands of people on Facebook shows police carrying a victim through a parking lot on a cloth stretcher. Another shows officers giving medical attention to a person on the ground by flashlight as people shout all around. Still another shows a swarm of police in all directions managing a crowd of bystanders. Trash litters the scene from where people fled in panic as bystanders talk about someone being hit in the head and another being shot in the back. "Everybody ran; everybody cleared off," a person can be heard saying. People also began coming to grips with the magnitude of the shooting on social media. "I can only imagine the level of panic and chaos that an incident of this magnitude may have caused. Beyond those directly affected by the shooting, my concern is that hundreds, perhaps even thousands, of people may have rushed to safety, potentially creating dangerous crowd surges and resulting in additional injuries," a pastor wrote on FAMU's Facebook page. "I sincerely pray that the number of injuries is minimal and that everyone affected is safe." ▶ Did you witness the shooting or its aftermath? Share your stories, photos or videos with us at news@tallahassee.com . Others took to social media to say their friends, family and loved ones were safe. "Praying for our kids because what I just witnessed at 7:50pm was unbelievable. My 1st and last homecoming. On God! My kids and their friends were crying and I'm trying to pull other people kids to safety," a witness wrote on Facebook. "This could have been any of our babies." A video taken earlier in the day before the gunfire showed massive crowds walking along Perry Street amid the homecoming festivities. 10:05 p.m. update: FSU issues alert to students: 'As a precaution,' stay indoors At 10 p.m., Florida State University issued an "Emergency Message for the Florida State University Tallahassee Campus" with the extraordinary advice to avoid going outside on a weekend evening. "Florida State University is aware of reports of an off-campus shooting near Bragg Stadium on the FAMU campus in Tallahassee earlier this evening (Sat. Oct 24). At this time, there is no indication that members of the FSU community were involved. As a precaution, students, faculty and staff in the Tallahassee area are advised to remain indoors this evening and stay alert. The university will provide additional information as appropriate." This is an Emergency Message for the Florida State University Tallahassee Campus. Florida State University is aware of reports of an off-campus shooting near Bragg Stadium on the FAMU campus in Tallahassee earlier this evening (Sat. Oct 24). At this t https://t.co/M1KzwIWsgV — FSU Alert (@FSUAlert) October 25, 2026 10 p.m.: TPD says scene is secure; no word on victims Alicia Hill with the Tallahassee Police Department told the Tallahassee Democrat at 9:45 p.m. that the scene was secure. She had not additional information about the number of victims or extent of injuries. She also could not say specifically where the gunfire occurred on Perry Street. TPD's online crime tracking map notes an 8:02 p.m. call to "Assist Other Agencies" at Perry and Manatee Streets, which is an intersection next to Bragg Stadium. FAMU posted at about 10 p.m. "TPD is investigating a shooting on Perry Street. The number of victims and extent of injuries are unknown. Please avoid the area while officers investigate." 9:15 p.m. UPDATE: TPD reports shooting on Perry Street with victims after FAMU issues 'shelter in place alert' The Tallahassee Police Department (TPD) posted on social media that it "is currently investigating a shooting on Perry Street. At this time, the number of victims and the extent of their injuries are unknown." "Community members are encouraged to avoid the area while officers conduct their investigation," the post on social media said. The news broke during a busy Florida A&M homecoming weekend and shortly after the Rattlers lost their homecoming game to Arkansas-Pine Bluff. The university sent out a campus safety alert at 8:40 p.m. to "shelter in place" and avoid the area near Bragg Stadium. TPD spokesperson Alicia Hill was heading to the scene but had no additional information other than to say "there certainly are victims." Hill said TPD was closing down Perry Street, and she said the agency would provide more updates when information was available. As news of the shooting spread, people who were on Perry Street began to post on social media what they saw. "Perry St was wild tonight. Running, falling, ducking and hiding," one person wrote. "They literally just shot these ppl in front of me," another person wrote. "Yall please pray for they families." A Tallahassee Democrat photojournalist said she heard a lot of sirens coming from multiple directions at about 8:15 p.m. She heard fire engines heading over probably 7-10 minutes later, and flying above were multiple police drones overhead headed toward Bragg. ORIGINAL STORY Florida A&M University issued a public safety alert Saturday night warning people to avoid the area around Bragg Memorial Stadium because of police activity. “FAMU Alert: Police activity near Bragg Stadium and perry street. Avoid the area or shelter in place if nearby,” the university said in the social media alert. The alert was posted at about 8:40 p.m., shortly after FAMU’s homecoming football loss. FAMU Alert: Police activity near Bragg Stadium and perry street . Avoid the area or shelter in place if nearby. — Florida A&M University (@FAMU_1887) October 25, 2026 The university did not immediately provide details about what prompted the police response or whether anyone had been injured. A Tallahassee Police Department Watch commander was not immediately available. People near Bragg Stadium and Perry Street were advised either to avoid the area or shelter in place. This is a developing story. Check back for updates. articles.title: 'Weaponizing the law': California AG slams DOJ's attack on alleged noncitizen voting
articles.summary: People cast their ballots at St Mary's Episcopal church during the first day of early voting in Los Angeles, California, on Saturday. Photograph: Chris Torres/EPA California’s attorney general on Saturday rebuked the Trump administration’s efforts to quash alleged noncitizen voting, calling it “politicizing and weaponizing the law”. Rob Bonta, the state’s attorney general, said the justice department acted at Donald Trump’s direction. “It is once again the United States Department of Justice politicizing and weaponizing the law to attack its enemies, and it is completely improper,” he told MS Now. Less than two weeks before the midterms, federal prosecutors called upon California election officials to verify within 48 hours a list of about 20,000 ballots belonging to suspected noncitizens. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare , but in the run-up to the midterm elections, the justice department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. California’s election personnel have raised concern that the administration’s directive could disenfranchise citizens. Los Angeles officials said this week a “high percentage” of the individuals on the list were born in the United States. “Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted – and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” California’s governor Gavin Newsom posted on social media . “Voter intimidation has no place in our democracy,” Pete Aguilar, a congressman representing south-west San Bernardino county, said in a social media post . The federal government’s oversight attempts come amid a national Republican effort to crack down on alleged voter fraud, particularly any cases among undocumented immigrants. “We are asking each county election official to commit to working with us by providing the necessary information for DHS to quickly verify citizenship status. With their help, we can ensure the most secure election in California history,” the justice department said. Bonta, the California attorney general, has raised questions about the evidence behind the suspected noncitizen ballots. “All they provided was a list of people and nothing about why they’re purportedly ineligible. If they have such information, we would be happy to review it, but they’ve provided none,” Bonta said at a recent press conference. The DoJ also charged 28 foreign nationals recently, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote. “Today’s arrests prove what we have been saying,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, said in a statement. “California is mailing ballots to noncitizens, and they are refusing to comply with federal law, which makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote. The voting rights of American citizens must be protected.” The defendants are lawful permanent residents, who have legal status in the US but are not citizens authorized to vote. Some state officials took no action on Friday’s letters, citing the fast-approaching election, which spurred a legal battle with the justice department. An appeals court is set to hear the matter on Tuesday. articles.title: 价格打折，哪些股票超跌了？
articles.summary: 双十一，股市也开启了“打折促销”。近期市场快速调整，创业板指从4372点回落到2700点以下，科创综指来到1300附近。不少前期热门股票大幅回撤，以历史高点为参照，中际旭创、新易盛、东山精密等热门股价格已跌至约四折。 尽管10月23日市场明显反弹，但科技成长板块此前的调整幅度已经不小，也引发了市场对科技股是否会重演周期股大幅波动的担忧。 股票毕竟不是普通商品，价格打折不等于估值便宜。 从交易层面看，下跌太快，股价反而可能出现反弹。但这类交易性反弹，并不是我们要讨论的“超跌”。 我们所说“超跌”是基于完整盈利周期基础上的估值便宜。 投资者在这个价格上购买股票，可能会输掉一些时间，但不会丧失本金。 为此，我们拿出光伏，锂电的龙头，跟光通信龙头进行比较。光伏和锂电都有完整的周期可以参考。 通过选取隆基绿能、宁德时代和中际旭创作为典型案例，比较不同景气阶段下的盈利和估值变化，观察经历大幅调整后，当前股价是否已经出现估值超跌。 看PE、PB的历史分位，不能判断估值 股价大幅调整后，市场通常把PE、PB放到历史的维度里去比较 ：当前低于历史多少分位，就说股票有多便宜。 例如，仅看原始PE的分布，宁德时代截至今年9月30日，15.85倍的pe低于此前五年20个季度的全部观测值；中际旭创当前32倍估值处于历史40%分位水平。单看历史估值，宁德时代似乎已经比较便宜，中际旭创也不算贵。 但问题是，这一估值背后所对应的盈利并不相同。 对于景气波动较大的公司，历史估值分位未必能反映真实的估值水平。仅是用历史分位，很难判断在周期中，是否真的“超跌”。 行业景气高低点，企业盈利水平差异明显 周期股在景气高点和低谷的盈利差异往往很大。即期估值容易受到利润波动的影响。 把三家公司利润放在一起来进行对比，通过年末EPS和ROE的观察，对周期差异就有更直观的感觉。 隆基2022年末ROE还有23.8%，2026年二季度却降至-15.5%，EPS也转为负数；中际旭创2021年末ROE只有7.6%，2026年二季度已超过51%，EPS从约1元增至13.4元；宁德时代的EPS则从2021年末约4.3元增加到2026年二季度约17.1元。 景气高点，利润增长会压低PE；景气低谷，利润收缩甚至亏损，又会使PE大幅抬升或失去参考意义。这就是单看即期PE容易踩的“坑”。 因此，仅凭PE、PB的历史分位，难以准确判断股价是否超跌。 我们尝试以历史稳态ROE为基准，还原企业在正常盈利水平下的估值，进一步观察当前股价是否具备安全边际。 估值是否合理，需要考虑完整的景气周期 经历大幅调整后， 优质公司的股价是否已经跌至具有吸引力的位置，需要从完整的行业景气周期出发，以正常盈利水平为参照。 我们采用历史ROE中位数作为稳态盈利水平，据此测算修正后的EPS和PE，观察企业在正常盈利能力下的历史估值区间，进而判断当前股价是否具备估值安全边际。 三家公司，三个答案 我们以三家公司各自的盈利周期起始日为起点，选取此后26个季度的ROE（TTM）中位数作为稳态盈利参考，并据此修正历史EPS和PE。 这样剔除不同景气阶段盈利波动对PE的影响，在相对统一的盈利水平下，观察市场过去给予企业的估值是否合理。 隆基绿能：便宜的前提，是先把利润赚回来 隆基的历史样本为2016Q1—2022Q2。26个季度的ROE中位数为19.53%，对应的标准化PE中位数为26.43倍。 问题是，隆基目前仍在亏损，负PE已经没法正常比较。按2026Q3的11.21元股价倒推：如果未来ROE恢复到约7.22%，对应PE为26.43倍；如果恢复到历史中位数19.53%，对应PE约9.76倍。 对隆基来说，能不能恢复盈利、能恢复到什么水平，比股价跌了多少更重要。 宁德时代：把盈利调回常态后，估值仍偏低 宁德的历史样本为2018Q2—2024Q3。ROE中位数为13.48%，标准化PE中位数为49.12倍，历史25%—75%区间为36.79—81.43倍。 2026Q3，宁德时代PE为15.85倍。把当期ROE折回13.48%后，修正PE约26.64倍，仍低于历史区间下沿，处在历史约3.8%分位。 换句话说，宁德的低PE并不只是当下盈利较高造成的。即使用历史中位数ROE来算，估值相对过去仍然偏低，具备一定的历史估值吸引力。 中际旭创：PE不高，不代表安全垫已经很厚 中际的历史样本为2020Q1—2026Q2。ROE中位数为10.73%，标准化PE中位数为61.95倍。 只看当前32倍PE，它处在原始PE历史约34.6%分位，处于较低分位水平。但如果用历史ROE中位数来折算，当前示意标准化PE约153倍，处于历史约84.6%分位，超过历史中间50%区间。 两种口径之所以差这么多，关键在于对高ROE能持续多久的判断。 如果未来ROE逐渐回到历史水平，当前价格在这套模型下没有明显的绝对吸引力；但如果AI光模块需求带来的高盈利能维持较长时间，用10.73%的历史ROE做假设又可能过于保守。 跌下来以后，究竟怎样才算便宜？ 三家公司给出了不同的答案：宁德时代在盈利还原至历史中枢后，估值仍处于历史较低分位；隆基绿能的估值吸引力取决于盈利修复；中际旭创则需要关注当前高ROE的持续性。 从跨周期估值角度看，判断股价是否超跌，不能仅依据股价回撤幅度或短期交易性反弹，更需要考察企业在稳态盈利水平下的估值位置。 若盈利回归常态后，估值仍明显偏高，说明当前价格对盈利回落的风险反映可能不足；若在相对保守的盈利假设下，估值仍处于历史低位，则可能具备一定的安全边际，但仍需结合基本面判断折价是否合理。 不过需要注意的是，历史中位数不能代替未来盈利预测，行业景气和公司竞争力也可能发生变化。但把价格与可持续的赚钱能力放在一起看，至少能避免把“跌得多”直接当成“够便宜”。 股价打了几折不重要。重要的是，利润回到正常水平以后，价格是否依然合理。 本文来源： 东吴证券陈李、葛晓媛 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: AI势头回落并非牛熊分界
articles.summary: AI趋势回落并非熊市开端，非AI可能反而会面临更为有利的环境 1）产业趋势回落≠牛转熊。A股在过往存在比较广泛的“产业趋势回落=牛转熊”的思维，核心是过往的产业趋势（2006~2007年的工业与金融、2009年的地产与基建、2013~2015年的移动互联、2019~2021年的能源转型等）对其他经济部门带来广泛的拉动作用。而本轮AI产业的进展，至少在短期内对其他经济部门产生了不少挤出效应，包括导致了物料和资源价格暴涨、推动了债券市场供需紧张和长债利率大幅飙升、一定程度上挤出就业，财富效应的增长极为失衡，市场分化的程度历史罕见，甚至出现了所谓“硅基世界”和“碳基世界”的对立。这也意味着，过往“产业趋势行情结束=牛转熊”的经验可能并不适用于这轮AI硬件主导的行情，非AI的不少板块早已步入下行趋势，而AI只不过最后“补跌”。 2）AI短期内对其他部门产生了负外部性，若AI势头回落，一些非AI板块反而可能有转机。目前已经显性化的负外部性至少包含三类：第一，电子元器件、电力等基础生活物资的大幅涨价，抬高生产和生活成本，压抑其他领域需求，典型的如消费电子；第二，算力基础设施投建推动私人部门巨额债务融资，推升全球无风险利率，对所有高利率敏感性的需求产生冲击；第三，挤出就业，尤其是对于年轻人就业的影响，比如根据斯坦福与ADP就业数据库今年9月最新数据，自动化型AI使用占比最高职业组的22~25岁就业较2022年11月下降10.9%，最低组同期上升7.8%。这些因素引发了实体经济和市场的剧烈分化，但反过来看，如果AI投资的速度在未来有所放缓，非AI板块可能也不会面临如此负面的宏观环境，比如无风险利率出现大幅回落。事实上，从当前的美债定价来看，10年期美债利率的走向与北美AI硬件股的股价走势高度相关，如果未来出现持续性的回落，至少对海外的非AI部门需求可能产生促进。 估值收缩的进程今年已基本完成，行情宽度有望逐步拓展 1）AI的二阶导修正、非AI的估值收缩，都有望在今年基本完成。AI完成了第一波“二阶导”修正。与2021年底至2022年4月底的新能源行情调整类似，本轮AI同样是在产业景气仍在、增速预期转弱时提前下修估值。从估值收缩的视角出发，本轮AI硬件的估值压缩幅度已与2022年新能源第一轮调整相当。根据Wind数据，7月1日以来，电子与通信板块整体法PE（TTM）从74.0倍压缩至42.4倍，降幅42.8%；2022年新能源第一轮调整（2021年12月17日-2022年4月26日），电力设备及新能源板块市值下PE从51.2倍压缩至27.8倍，降幅45.7%。站在全球对比的视角下，A股非AI板块处于全球估值洼地。我们用中、美、日、韩四个市场的AI与非AI龙头篮子，以整体法测算PE（TTM）并进行跨市场对比。截至10月22日，A股是唯一一个AI相对非AI估值溢价仍高于历史中枢的市场：AI/非AI的PE倍数为4.4倍，处于2016年以来82%的分位，美、日、韩的这一倍数则分别回落至1%、17%、24%的分位。美、日非AI非金融龙头的PE分别为33.5倍和23.0倍，处于98%和95%的分位；A股非AI非金融龙头只有15.6倍，处于历史21%分位，消费、制造、医药龙头分别只处于12%、1%、3%的分位。当然，低估值源于疲弱的内需以及市场对非AI领域外需的潜在担忧（贸易摩擦、海外高利率、高油价等），有其合理性。但换个角度看，这种导致低估值的悲观，很大程度上源于今年的现实与年初市场期待的巨大割裂，投资者难以预料在“十五五”的第一年广义财政赤字会意外转为大幅负增长、市场从美联储降息预期转为加息预期、10年期美债利率创了2007年以来新高、中欧贸易摩擦突然升温、美伊战争爆发且持续快一年。这种落差，是导致不少非AI板块在今年业绩增长亮眼的情况下估值发生剧烈收缩的原因。当下，至少市场已经充分认知到了这些宏观负面因素，无论是海外利率还是国内政策，任何边际上超预期的变化可能都有助于改变当下A股相对于全球市场更为悲观的估值体系。 2）K型分化逐步收敛，行情宽度有望逐步拓展。对于AI侧，商业化空间增长焦虑还将继续约束AI投资单年度的绝对规模体量，同时加深市场对于未来“一阶导”拐点的警惕，AI对于非AI板块的虹吸很难再出现，同时考虑到主流机构资金仍然超配TMT板块，市场反弹过程中的持仓均衡化过程也将制约AI板块的弹性。我们看到，在本周市场止跌企稳的过程中，率先反弹的AI新技术是筹码出清相当彻底且机构持仓比例低的机器人板块，而非算力基建相关的板块。对非AI板块，当下几乎所有的负面因素都已经被市场所认知（即便可能并未完全定价），在经历一轮系统性调整后，低预期本身就是有利的条件。以出海板块为例，中欧贸易摩擦已经摆在台面上，未来每年的规则修订谈判和博弈可能是常态化的，企业最终还是会凭借强大的竞争优势适应；人民币在明年只要升值速度有所放缓，汇兑损失就会同比减少，就会带来净利润率的回升；美国中期选举后民主党如果控制国会，中东战争格局可能会有积极变化，所带来的油价影响可能边际上转弱；AI投资增速放缓，带来海外长端无风险利率回落，对非AI行业的需求抑制作用减弱。由于这些负面因素在今年已经被投资者系统性认知，只要后续有边际上的好转，对非AI板块本身也产生促进。 资金面的出清需要时间，PB-ROE 代表的稳健回报型策略可能更加占优 资金面快速恶化的过程大概率已接近尾声，在本周ETF明显放量的信号下，主动买盘开始谨慎流入市场，融资盘去杠杆的负向循环被阻断。截至10月21日，两市融资余额已回落至2.45万亿元，相对年内高点累计减少5600亿元，降幅18.6%，已回到去年11月下旬的水平，交易层面的降温更为明显，融资买入额占两市成交额的比例（MA5，下同）6月平均为9.86%，7月降至8.99%，9月为8.66%，10月以来进一步降至8.01%，10月16日读数7.84%，为2024年9月以来的最低值，低于“9.24”行情前约9%的水平。活跃私募的仓位同样回到低位，对中信证券渠道调研显示，样本活跃私募仓位8月7日当周以来持续回落，10月16日已降至67.5%，为2024年3月以来最低，较76.3%的历史中位数低8.8个百分点。虽然资金面指标已经回落到较低的位置，但彻底出清并开始持续改善仍然需要时间，这个阶段动量和景气策略会持续弱势，市场轮动速度加快，而以PB-ROE外代表的低估值质量型策略会更占优。目前有两类行业在明年满足这样的框架，一类是具备高股息率和稳健盈利增速的品种，如白电、纺织服装、食品调味、火电等，另一类是带有供给出清潜力逻辑的品种，如油运、快递物流、头部地产开发商、部分锂电材料、石化偏中游的环节等。 articles.title: SemiAnalysis创始人深度解析：AI投资还能撑多久？英伟达护城河还能守住吗？内存荒何时结束？
articles.summary: AI基础设施投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本上升、半导体供应链受限与自研芯片竞争加剧，正在共同考验这轮AI热潮的持续性。 在10月23日于美国举行的CASPA第35届年度大会上，SemiAnalysis创始人兼CEO Dylan Patel、Bernstein董事总经理兼高级分析师 Stacy Rasgon，以及Austin Lyons围绕半导体行业前景展开讨论，重点涉及AI基础设施投资、供应链瓶颈与芯片竞争格局。 Patel指出， 当前AI算力需求依然旺盛，但基板、内存等关键环节的产能约束，正在限制基础设施扩张。 与此同时，融资成本大幅攀升，缺乏长期客户订单的新兴云服务商越来越难以获得资金，AI投资能否持续推进，不仅取决于需求，也取决于项目的融资能力与回报。 对于英伟达，Rasgon认为，其产品性能提升仍能支撑较高售价，但云厂商自研芯片正在改变竞争格局。 随着Google TPU、亚马逊Trainium以及OpenAI等企业的自研芯片计划推进，英伟达即使继续增长，也可能面临市场份额和定价能力的双重压力。 内存市场则面临另一重考验：HBM需求旺盛、行业利润率处于高位，但厂商扩产可能在2028年后逐步改变供需关系。未来两年，融资能力、关键零部件供给与自研芯片的竞争，将成为影响AI基础设施扩张速度和产业链利润分配的关键变量。 华尔街见闻总结要点如下： AI投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本正成为重要约束。 美国10年期国债收益率突破5%，部分新兴云服务商无担保债券收益率接近15%。缺乏长期客户订单的企业融资难度更大，项目建设节奏将越来越取决于融资能力与投资回报。 半导体供应链瓶颈短期难解，基板与内存是关键制约。 基板、HBM、光学互联组件及洁净室产能均面临供应限制。相比之下，电力短缺可通过现场发电等方式部分缓解，半导体供应链扩产则需要更长时间。 内存短缺可能延续至新增产能释放，2028年后供需格局面临转折。 HBM需求旺盛，内存行业毛利率据称已达88%—90%；但如果新增产能在2028年后集中投产，而需求增速放缓，内存价格与利润率可能承压。 英伟达仍有性能优势，但自研芯片正在挑战其定价权。 英伟达持续通过性能提升支撑高售价，但Google
